title: Tommy Ridgley's Tra-la-la and the King contract dispute
summary: After leasing Tra-la-la to Decca, a telegram claimed Bartholomew's King contract auto-renewed, forcing a re-recording in New York with Lucky Millinder's band copying Dave's arrangement.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Yeah, I'm telling you, Jack Pearl, if you signed the contract Jack Pearl wrote for him, you were in trouble. I mean, you, for instance, just remember, for instance. I may have told you this earlier, but Tommy Ridgely's Tina Na, not Tina Na, what was it we did with Tommy Ridgely? It was one of the first things. It was a hit. Tra-la-la? Tra-la-la. Right. Tra-la-la. Well, Ridgely did Tra-la-la, and Dave and I did it, and leased it to Decca Records.
And the record came out, and Dave and I and Decca, of course, got telegrams from Jack Pearl that Dave was still on the contract. To King.

At the time, yeah. Yeah, but he wasn't on the contract. His contract had expired, but there was a thing in his contract that said it automatically renewed unless you wrote and said you didn't want it to renew.
Oh, one of those kind. Yeah. Unbelievable.
And, in fact, they forced us to re-record the song. Decca, Brotney, and Tommy. I'm never telling you the story now. We were the original Freedom Riders about that.
Right. We went up on a train. Train.
Yeah, but we went up there, and Lucky Millinder copied Dave's arrangement, and we re-recorded it with Lucky Millinder's band in Decca Studios.
